title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text: Code: github.com/Saminay786/transaction-risk-decision-framework · Status: in progress

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text:
What this project is about
Banks score every card transaction for fraud risk. But a score doesn’t stop fraud by itself. Someone still has to decide: approve the payment, send it to an analyst to review, or decline it.
This project builds that decision step. It combines the fraud probability, the transaction amount and the cost of each possible mistake, then picks the cheapest action for each transaction, without exceeding the number of reviews analysts can handle.
What to expect: a simple example of why a score isn’t enough, how each action is priced, four ways of deciding compared on unseen data, and how much we can trust the result.

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
section: How this differs from my IIT Madras project
text:
How this differs from my IIT Madras project
I first worked on this problem in a coursework project at IIT Madras: Credit Default and Fraud Risk Prediction (American Express – IIT Madras, 2022). I cleaned the data, balanced the classes with SMOTE-Tomek, and compared seven models. XGBoost did best on ROC-AUC and F1.
That project asked “how risky is this case?” This one asks what a risk team needs next: “what do we do about it, and what will it cost?”

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text:
Two transactions, same score
A €3 coffee and a €900 laptop both get a 10% fraud score. The common rule, “decline if the score is above 0.5”, approves both.
But if the laptop is fraud, the bank loses €900 plus fees. An analyst check costs about €5, which is clearly worth it for the laptop and not for the coffee. Same score, different right answer.

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text:
How it works
Data. The public ULB credit-card dataset: 284,807 European card transactions over two days, 492 of them fraud (0.17%).
Model. LightGBM, trained on the first 60% of the timeline and tested on the last 20%, as it would be used in real life. Unlike my coursework project, I didn’t oversample fraud. Oversampling inflates the scores, so a “10%” stops meaning 10%. Here the probability feeds a € calculation, so it has to be honest.
Pricing each action. With p = fraud probability and A = amount:
approve = p × (A + fees)
review  = analyst cost + p × (share analysts miss) × (A + fees) + (1 − p) × customer delay
decline = (1 − p) × (lost margin + cost of an annoyed customer)
For the laptop: €92 to approve, €15 to review, €33 to decline, so it goes to review. For the coffee: €1.80 to approve, so it goes through. The cost inputs (€5 per review, 90% of fraud caught on review, and so on) are assumptions that a real bank’s Finance team would supply.
Four ways of deciding:

P0: approve everything (the cost of doing nothing)
P1: decline if p > 0.5 (the common default)
P2: two cut-offs, tuned on past data
P3: the cheapest action per transaction, within a review cap of 1%

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text:
Results



Total cost per 1,000 test transactions. Black lines show the 95% range.






P1: decline if p > 0.5
P3: cheapest action




Cost per 1,000 transactions
€89.8
€69.4


Share of fraud € stopped
49%
68%


Analyst reviews used
0
33 (of 569 allowed)



P3 wins by doing exactly what the laptop example suggests: it spends a few reviews on risky, expensive transactions that the 0.5 rule lets through.
How sure are we? The test period has only 75 frauds, so I resampled it 1,000 times. P3 beats approving everything in 99.7% of resamples, and beats the 0.5 rule in 85%. The second gain is promising but not proven: its 95% range is −€352 to €3,493. I’d use it to justify a pilot, not to promise savings.
A surprise. P2, the tuned cut-offs, did slightly worse than the plain 0.5 rule. It was tuned on just 33 frauds, so it mostly fitted noise. P3 has nothing to tune, which helps when fraud examples are scarce.
If analysts cost more? Raising the review cost from €1 to €20, P3 uses fewer reviews (133 down to 4), and its cost stays around €67–70 per 1,000, against €90 for the 0.5 rule.

title: The €3 Coffee and the €900 Laptop
text:
Limitations and next steps
The costs are assumptions, there are few frauds, and the data covers only two days with no customer IDs. Next, I’d move the same decision layer to the larger IEEE-CIS dataset, keep each customer in only one of training or testing, and simulate chargebacks arriving weeks later, as they do in practice.
The takeaway: a fraud model’s job is to estimate risk. Deciding what to do with that risk is a separate job, and it’s where most of the money is.
Full details, formulas and a one-page decision memo are in the GitHub repo.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
The problem
Retailers spend a lot on promotions. The common way to judge them is “units sold during the promo vs. a normal week”. That number mixes up three things: the discount itself, the display or mailer that usually comes with it, and sales that would have happened anyway. Plan from it, and you over-invest in discounts.
The project works through four questions in order:








Step
Question
Method




1. Measure
How much extra volume does a discount actually cause?
Double Machine Learning


2. Decide
Which product should get which discount, in which week?
Integer optimisation (CP-SAT)


3. Cross-check
Does a top-down view agree?
Bayesian marketing mix model


4. Test
How would we prove it works in real stores?
A/B test design: power simulation + CUPED



Data: dunnhumby’s The Complete Journey, with two years of grocery transactions from ~2,500 households plus display and mailer data. I used the 137 top-revenue products over 99 weeks (11,892 product-weeks), excluding fuel, gift cards and miscellaneous items.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
section: 1. Measure: what does a discount really cause?
text:
1. Measure: what does a discount really cause?
I built a product × week panel. The treatment is discount depth. The controls are display/mailer exposure, past sales, seasonality and how much else in the category was on promo. I then estimated the effect with Double ML (EconML LinearDML, LightGBM, 5-fold cross-fitting) and compared it with a naive estimate and a placebo test.




Elasticity θ
What 10% off does




Naive (no controls)
3.49
+42% units


Double ML
2.51 (95% CI 2.18–2.85)
+29% units


Placebo test
0.01
no effect, as expected



About 43.8% of promo volume was non-incremental. Those were sales the retailer would have made anyway.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
2. Decide: build the promo calendar
The per-category effects feed an integer program (OR-Tools CP-SAT). It picks a discount (10/20/30% or none) for each product-week, subject to a budget, weekly promo slots, a frequency cap, a per-category cap and no back-to-back promos. I compared it with a common rule of thumb: deepest discount on the top sellers.
Same $5k budget, 8 weeks, 10 promo slots per week:




Incremental margin
Budget used




“Deepest discount on top sellers”
$60
full


Optimised calendar
$719
37% less



The rule of thumb loses mostly because it puts deep discounts on products that would sell anyway. Treat the absolute dollar figure with caution: step 3 suggests it’s overstated.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
3. Cross-check: the category view
As a top-down check, I modelled weekly category sales for 8 categories with a Bayesian marketing mix model (PyMC-Marketing). It has three levers (discount rate, mailers, displays) and accounts for carryover and diminishing returns.



Margin returned per dollar of retailer discount, by category (Bayesian MMM, 94% credible intervals).



Discount ROI is below 1 in 7 of 8 categories. Soft drinks return about $0.69 per $1 of discount. Only frozen pizza is above break-even (1.24), and even there the interval is wide.
Displays look cheap to break even on (roughly $0.005–0.08 per placement). That hints at moving some discount money into displays, depending on costs I don’t have.
Both models rank the categories the same way. But the category-level effect is only 43–55% of the product-level one for bread, cheese and soft drinks (19% for deli meats). That fits with discounts partly stealing sales from other products in the same category (cannibalisation). So the optimiser’s gain is probably about half what step 2 says.
Model health: 0 divergences, max r-hat 1.008, R² 0.44–0.64 for 7 of 8 categories.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
section: 4. Test: how would we prove it works?
text:
4. Test: how would we prove it works?
A model’s prediction isn’t proof. Before rolling out the calendar, a retailer would want to test it, so I designed the experiment:

Design: randomly split stores 50/50. Treatment stores run the optimised calendar, and control stores keep current practice.
Unit: stores, not shoppers, because a promo calendar applies to everyone who shops in a store. The data has 582 stores. The 137 planned products sell in 115 of them, and 84 have enough weekly sales to include.
Metric: weekly promo margin per store on the planned products.
Analysis: compare the groups with a t-test, using CUPED to adjust for each store’s margin in the 8 weeks before the test. Big stores stay big, so removing that predictable part cuts the noise.

Then I checked the design on real history: 84 stores, with 1,000 simulated tests per scenario.
Is the analysis trustworthy? I ran “A/A tests”: random splits with no real change. The test raised a false alarm 4–6% of the time, which matches the 5% it should.
How big an effect could it detect? I added known lifts to the treatment stores and counted how often the test caught them:



Chance an 8-week test detects a given true lift, with and without CUPED (1,000 simulations each, real store data).










Answer




Smallest lift detectable 80% of the time (8 weeks, CUPED)
≈13% (12% at 12 weeks, 15% at 4 weeks)


Without CUPED
never reaches 80%, even at a 15% lift


Optimiser’s predicted gain vs. current practice
≈3% (≈1.6% if step 3 is right)


Chance of detecting 3% with this test
≈10%


Stores needed to detect 3%
≈1,500



What this means:

With these stores, a test would almost always say “no significant effect”, even if the calendar works. That result shouldn’t be read as the calendar failing.
CUPED matters a lot here. It roughly triples the chance of detecting a real effect.
The real fix is a bigger or less noisy test: full-store sales instead of a 2,500-household panel (here each store sees only ~100 panel households, while a real store likely serves far more), a metric that pools more categories, a longer test, or a switchback design.

It’s much better to learn this before running a test than after.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
Limitations

Observational data. The Double ML estimate is causal only if the controls capture everything that drives both promo decisions and sales.
No cost data. Margin is assumed to be 30% of shelf price, and suppliers are assumed to fund 50% of the discount. Display and mailer costs are unknown.
The optimiser likely over-credits discounts. Cannibalisation is handled only by a simple category cap, and pull-forward (shoppers stocking up) only by a “no back-to-back promos” rule.
The test simulation is simplified. It applies the lift evenly to the store metric, and panel stores only see panel households’ purchases. The method transfers to a real retailer, but the store count doesn’t.
The MMM has 82 weeks per category, and mailers and displays often run together, so their separate effects are uncertain.

title: Promo Optimization Engine
text:
What’s next

Scale the product-level effects by a category-level factor, so the optimiser stops over-crediting discounts.
Model pull-forward directly instead of using a rule.
Extend the test design with a switchback (alternating weeks) and stratified store assignment, and compare their power.
